claims.text: Under tribo-corrosion, degradation of the high-entropy alloy is governed by mechanical removal of its protective passive oxide film during sliding.
Removal of the passive film exposes the underlying alloy.
Exposure of the underlying alloy triggers accelerated, localized corrosion.
Corrosion acts synergistically with wear to increase total material loss relative to static corrosion.
The alloy initially has a uniform, intact passive oxide film.
Sliding mechanically removes or damages the passive film.
Fresh alloy surface exposed by sliding undergoes rapid, localized corrosion.
Breakdown of passivity accelerates corrosion.
Corrosion damage weakens the alloy's resistance to wear.
Coupling passive-film breakdown, corrosion, and wear produces a synergistic increase in overall degradation.
Tribo-corrosion will produce greater total degradation than static immersion in the same electrolyte.
Tribo-corrosion will produce a higher corrosion component because of continuous passive-film removal.
Corrosion-induced softening may enhance the wear rate.
Under static immersion, the passive film remains largely intact.
The predicted mechanism should apply when passive-film protection dominates and loading disrupts the film without causing complete plastic deformation.
The prediction may fail when the alloy rapidly repassivates.
The prediction may fail when degradation mechanisms other than passive-film disruption dominate.
The quantitative synergy may depend on microstructural heterogeneity and repassivation kinetics.
Passive-film integrity, mass loss, wear-track depth, and corrosion current density can be compared between static immersion and controlled sliding conditions.
Failure to observe increased corrosion current density, mass loss, or passive-film disruption under sliding would falsify passive-film removal as the driver of synergistic degradation.
